title: TCP vs UDP
subtitle: Comparing connection-oriented reliable byte streams (3-way handshake, congestion control) against connectionless low-overhead datagrams.
keyTakeaways: TCP guarantees reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery via a 3-way handshake, sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmissions, and congestion control.
UDP is a connectionless 'fire-and-forget' datagram protocol with an 8-byte header, zero handshake RTT, and no Transport-Layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking.
For real-time media (WebRTC, VoIP, FPS gaming), a retransmitted late TCP packet is worse than a dropped UDP packet because stalls destroy live interactivity.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) creates a virtual full-duplex pipe between two sockets. Before sending a single byte of application payload, TCP requires a 3-way handshake (`SYN`, `SYN-ACK`, `ACK`), costing 1 full Round-Trip Time (RTT). During transmission, TCP numbers every byte, requires receiver acknowledgments (`ACK`), and enforces both **Flow Control** (via the receiver's advertised sliding window so a fast sender doesn't overwhelm a slow receiver) and **Congestion Control** (slow start, CUBIC, or Google BBR to avoid collapsing intermediate internet routers).
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: TCP guarantees reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery via a 3-way handshake, sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmissions, and congestion control.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: UDP is a connectionless 'fire-and-forget' datagram protocol with an 8-byte header, zero handshake RTT, and no Transport-Layer Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for TCP vs UDP:
bullets: **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)**: Provides guaranteed delivery and strict ordering out-of-the-box, battle-tested congestion control (bbr/cubic), universally traverses firewalls. Best suited for REST/gRPC APIs, database connections (Postgres/Redis), file transfers, web pages (HTTP/1.1 & HTTP/2), and chat messages.

**UDP (User Datagram Protocol)**: Provides zero connection setup delay, minimal 8-byte packet header, no hol blocking, app controls what to drop vs retransmit. Best suited for Live video/voice calls (WebRTC/Zoom), multiplayer real-time games, DNS lookups, and HTTP/3 (QUIC).

TCP Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking: Because TCP guarantees strict byte ordering, if packet #4 is lost on the wire, packets #5, #6, and #7 sit locked inside the OS kernel buffer until #4 is retransmitted.
Nagle's Algorithm vs `TCP_NODELAY`: Nagle buffers small writes to coalesce packets; latency-sensitive apps set `TCP_NODELAY` to flush immediately.
Zero Handshake Latency: Data flows on the very first packet.
No HoL Blocking Across Independent Frames: A dropped video delta frame doesn't block an incoming audio packet or player position update.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply TCP vs UDP across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for REST/gRPC APIs, database connections (Postgres/Redis), file transfers, web pages (HTTP/1.1 & HTTP/2), and chat messages, suited for environments requiring Guaranteed delivery and strict ordering out-of-the-box, battle-tested congestion control (BBR/CUBIC), universally traverses firewalls.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Live video/voice calls (WebRTC/Zoom), multiplayer real-time games, DNS lookups, and HTTP/3 (QUIC), where Zero connection setup delay, minimal 8-byte packet header, no HoL blocking, app controls what to drop vs retransmit.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: User Datagram Protocol (UDP) adds almost nothing on top of IP except source/destination ports and a checksum: just an 8-byte header compared to TCP's 20–60 bytes. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of TCP vs UDP introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: 1-rtt handshake overhead, transport-layer head-of-line blocking stalls entire connection on a single lost packet, heavier kernel state.

**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: packets can arrive out of order, duplicated, or vanish silently; some corporate firewalls block raw udp ports.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for TCP vs UDP:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: For real-time media (WebRTC, VoIP, FPS gaming), a retransmitted late TCP packet is worse than a dropped UDP packet because stalls destroy live interactivity.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: When designing Zoom, Discord, or an online game, explicitly contrast control plane vs media plane: 'We use TCP (HTTPS/WebSockets) for authentication, room signaling, and text chat where reliability is mandatory, and UDP (WebRTC/SRTP) for live audio/video streams where low latency beats 100% packet delivery.'
